name: Aldo Rossi
bio: Rossi mattered twice over: first as the theorist of L'architettura della città (1966), which argued that the city is a repository of collective memory built from persistent types, and then as the designer who gave that argument melancholy built form. His palette barely changed — cones, cubes, square windows, striped porticoes — whether the commission was a cemetery, a floating theatre or an espresso pot for Alessi. The San Cataldo cemetery at Modena, won in competition with Gianni Braghieri in 1971 and still unfinished, remains the key monument of the Tendenza he led. He taught in Milan, Zurich and Venice, and in 1990 became the first Italian to win the Pritzker. He died in 1997 of injuries from a car crash, leaving the 'analogous city' as one of postwar architecture's most quoted ideas.

projects.title: San Cataldo Cemetery
projects.blurb: A roofless ossuary cube and blue-roofed colonnades — a city of the dead, deliberately unfinished.

projects.title: Teatro del Mondo
projects.blurb: A floating timber theatre towed into the lagoon for the 1980 Biennale, then dismantled; his most loved building barely existed.

projects.title: Monte Amiata Housing, Gallaratese
projects.blurb: A 182-meter housing slab on a rhythmic portico — the rationalist corridor block reduced to its type.

projects.title: Bonnefantenmuseum
projects.blurb: A brick E-plan museum on the Maas crowned by a zinc dome like a rocket nose.

projects.title: Teatro Carlo Felice
projects.blurb: The war-gutted opera house rebuilt behind its neoclassical portico, with a stone tower for a fly loft.

projects.title: Il Palazzo Hotel

projects.title: Quartier Schützenstrasse
projects.blurb: A city block reconstituted as a collage of invented facades, Palazzo Farnese quotation included.

projects.blurb: His only US building, finished posthumously on Broadway — cast-iron SoHo replayed in red steel and stone.

projects.title: Elementary School, Fagnano Olona
projects.blurb: A school arranged like a miniature civic square around a clock and an open-air theatre.

projects.title: Casa Aurora
projects.blurb: The GFT headquarters on a chamfered corner; Rossi's urban type-forms in brick and stone.

name: Arata Isozaki
bio: Isozaki was fourteen when Hiroshima burned across the shore from his hometown of Ōita; he later said his first experience of architecture was its absence. Trained under Kenzō Tange, he orbited Metabolism without ever joining it, then spent six decades refusing to settle into a style — brutalist library, mannerist museum, high-tech dome — treating each building as a fresh hypothesis. The Gunma museum and the Tsukuba Center made him Japan's leading postmodernist; MOCA in Los Angeles opened the American market to Japanese architects. He was also the profession's great kingmaker as juror and curator, famously rescuing Zaha Hadid's discarded Peak entry from the reject pile in 1983. The Pritzker finally arrived in 2019, decades after most people expected it; he died in 2022 at ninety-one.

projects.title: Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles
projects.blurb: Red sandstone vaults and a copper pyramid sunk into Bunker Hill; the building that introduced Isozaki to America.
projects.wikipedia: Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles

projects.title: Museum of Modern Art, Gunma
projects.blurb: An open lattice of twelve-meter cubes — the museum as pure gridded frame.

projects.title: Palau Sant Jordi
projects.blurb: The 17,000-seat arena for the 1992 Olympics, its domed space-frame roof assembled on the ground and jacked into place.

projects.title: Tsukuba Center Building
projects.blurb: A civic center for a new science city, quoting Michelangelo's Campidoglio in sunken reverse — Japanese postmodernism's set piece.

projects.title: Art Tower Mito
projects.blurb: An arts complex marked by a 100-meter helix of titanium tetrahedra, built for the city's centennial.

projects.title: Ōita Prefectural Library
projects.blurb: Brutalist concrete in his hometown, conceived through his theory of 'process planning' — a building designed to grow.

projects.title: Team Disney Building
projects.blurb: Corporate offices entered through the world's largest sundial; postmodern play at Disney scale.

projects.title: Qatar National Convention Centre
projects.blurb: A 250-meter facade held up by two colossal steel trees modeled on the sacred sidra.

projects.title: Nara Centennial Hall
projects.blurb: A gray-tiled ellipsoid concert hall, its hull deferring to the temple roofs of the old capital.

projects.title: Allianz Tower
projects.blurb: A 50-story tower of stacked curved-glass modules with Andrea Maffei — endlessness as a facade principle, delivered in his eighties.

name: Ricardo Legorreta
bio: Legorreta took the lesson of his friend and mentor Luis Barragán — walls, water, silence and saturated color — and scaled it from private gardens up to hotels, factories, libraries and whole campuses. The Camino Real hotel in Mexico City, built for the Olympic year of 1968, announced the method: a low labyrinth of pink and yellow planes instead of an international-style slab. He had founded Legorreta Arquitectos in 1965 after a decade with José Villagrán García, insisting Mexican architecture could be modern without being imported. From the 1980s he carried the vocabulary north, remaking Pershing Square in Los Angeles and giving San Antonio a library in 'enchilada red', and proved the palette traveled. He received the AIA Gold Medal in 2000 and the Praemium Imperiale in 2011, weeks before his death; his son Víctor continues the firm as LEGORRETA.

projects.title: Camino Real Hotel
projects.blurb: A five-hectare walled city of colored screens, fountains and patios; Mexican modernism at hotel scale, with Goeritz and Calder inside.

projects.title: San Antonio Central Library
projects.blurb: A stepped 'enchilada red' box that made a public library the most argued-about building in Texas.

projects.title: MARCO, Museo de Arte Contemporáneo
projects.blurb: Galleries around a water-filled patio at the foot of the Cerro de la Silla, entered past a giant Juan Soriano dove.
projects.wikipedia: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Monterrey

projects.title: Camino Real Ixtapa
projects.blurb: A resort terraced down a Pacific cliff like a manmade hillside village.

projects.title: Pershing Square
projects.blurb: Downtown LA's oldest park remade with a purple campanile, an aqueduct and an orange grove, with Laurie Olin.

projects.title: Papalote Museo del Niño
projects.blurb: A children's museum of blue-tiled geometric solids in Chapultepec Park.

projects.title: New Cathedral of Managua
projects.blurb: A concrete cathedral under 63 egg-crate domes, built to shrug off the earthquakes that destroyed its predecessor.

projects.title: Solana
projects.blurb: An IBM campus on the Texas prairie with Mitchell/Giurgola and Peter Walker — colored walls holding their own against the horizon.

projects.title: Fábrica Automex
projects.blurb: A Chrysler assembly plant with sculptural concrete towers by Mathias Goeritz; the early proof that industry could be emotional.

projects.title: Plaza Juárez
projects.blurb: The Foreign Ministry towers and a plaza of 1,034 red pyramids in a reflecting pool, facing the Alameda.

name: Peter Eisenman
bio: Newark-born, Cornell-trained, with a Cambridge PhD on formal syntax, Eisenman spent his first two decades treating architecture as a text to be read rather than a shelter to be lived in. He founded the Institute for Architecture and Urban Studies in 1967 and edited Oppositions, turning downtown Manhattan into the seminar room of American theory. His numbered 'cardboard' houses pursued grammar over comfort — the owners of House VI wrote a whole book about the difficulty of inhabiting it. Major built work came late: the Wexner Center's colliding grids in 1989, a Cincinnati design school, even an NFL stadium. The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin (2005), a tilting field of 2,711 concrete stelae, is that rare thing, theory that moves the public; the City of Culture of Galicia, halted unfinished in 2013, may be the most expensive essay ever built. Into his nineties, he is still teaching and still arguing.

projects.title: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
projects.blurb: 2,711 concrete stelae on an undulating grid beside the Brandenburg Gate; disorientation as commemoration.
projects.wikipedia: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe

projects.title: Wexner Center for the Arts
projects.blurb: A white scaffolding grid splicing two campus geometries; the first built manifesto of deconstructivism.

projects.title: City of Culture of Galicia
projects.blurb: A hilltop of quartzite waves generated from the old town's street plan; construction was halted in 2013 with two buildings unbuilt.

projects.title: House VI
projects.blurb: A weekend house as three-dimensional grammar exercise, complete with a slot bisecting the bedroom.

projects.title: Aronoff Center for Design and Art
projects.blurb: A design school of torqued, shifted segments threaded along an existing building's spine.
projects.wikipedia: Aronoff Center for Design and Art

projects.title: State Farm Stadium
projects.blurb: The Arizona Cardinals' barrel-shaped stadium with a retractable roof and a roll-out natural-grass field.

projects.title: Greater Columbus Convention Center
projects.blurb: A convention hall disguised as a row of pastel urban buildings, its plan derived from railway lines and fiber-optic cable.

projects.title: House II (Falk House)

projects.title: IBA Housing, Checkpoint Charlie

projects.title: Koizumi Sangyo Building
projects.blurb: A lighting company's headquarters with Eisenman's fractured grids erupting from a sober office block.

name: Richard Rogers
bio: Born in Florence in 1933 to an Anglo-Italian family, Rogers was dyslexic, drew badly, and compensated with conviction, charm and very good partners. At Yale he met Norman Foster; back in England they formed Team 4, the seedbed of British high-tech. In 1971, aged 38, he and Renzo Piano won the Pompidou competition with a building worn inside out — structure, ducts and escalators hung on the facade so the floors could stay free — and Lloyd's of London later repeated the move for the insurance market. The second half of his career was as much about cities as buildings: the Urban Task Force report, advisor to London mayors, a lifelong case for dense, compact, public urban life. He took the Pritzker in 2007, sat in the Lords as Lord Rogers of Riverside, wore fluorescent shirts to prove architecture need not be somber, and died in 2021.

projects.title: Centre Pompidou
projects.blurb: The inside-out culture machine designed with Renzo Piano — services color-coded on the facade, half the site left as public piazza.

projects.title: Lloyd's building
projects.blurb: The insurance market as oil rig: lifts, stairs and ducts pushed outside a soaring atrium. Grade I listed within 25 years.

projects.title: Madrid–Barajas Terminal 4
projects.blurb: A kilometer of undulating bamboo-lined roof on rainbow-painted branching steel; Stirling Prize 2006.

projects.title: Millennium Dome
projects.blurb: A kilometer-round Teflon tent hung from twelve yellow masts on the Greenwich peninsula — cheap per square meter, expensive politically.

projects.title: Senedd
projects.blurb: The Welsh parliament under a rippling timber roof, its glass walls a literal argument for transparent government.

projects.title: 122 Leadenhall Street
projects.blurb: The 'Cheesegrater' — a 224-meter wedge leaning back to protect the view of St Paul's.

projects.title: Heathrow Terminal 5
projects.blurb: Britain's biggest free-standing building at opening, a single-span waved roof over a 400-meter hall.

projects.title: European Court of Human Rights
projects.blurb: Twin drum chambers in steel and glass on the Ill — judicial architecture without a temple front.

projects.title: 3 World Trade Center
projects.blurb: An 80-story tower braced by external K-frames on the rebuilt Trade Center site.

projects.title: Bordeaux Law Courts
projects.blurb: Seven cedar-clad courtroom pods like wine vats under a floating glass-and-steel canopy.

name: Álvaro Siza
bio: Siza wanted to be a sculptor; architecture was the compromise his father would pay for, and the sculptor never quite left the work. He built his first projects in his twenties in Matosinhos, the fishing town where he was born — the Boa Nova tea house and the tidal pools at Leça, threaded into coastal rock so carefully that it is hard to say where design begins. After the 1974 revolution he built social housing with the SAAL brigades, residents at the table; with his teacher Fernando Távora he made the 'Porto School' shorthand for a modernism that carries the weight of place. The Pritzker came in 1992, the Serralves museum and the Expo 98 pavilion in the years after, and honors have not stopped since. Past ninety he still designs every project in soft pencil, and famously maintains no website — the drawings circulate anyway.

projects.title: Leça Swimming Pools
projects.blurb: Tidal pools set into the Atlantic rocks with low concrete walls; nature completed rather than replaced.

projects.title: Boa Nova Tea House
projects.blurb: A restaurant hugging the shore rocks under low timber ceilings; Siza at thirty, already unmistakable.

projects.title: Serralves Museum
projects.blurb: A white museum unfolding through an Art Deco estate's gardens, all controlled light and long approach.

projects.title: Pavilion of Portugal, Expo 98
projects.blurb: A 70-meter concrete canopy sagging like paper between two porticoes — impossibly thin, entirely calm.

projects.title: Church of Santa Maria
projects.blurb: A white parish church of tilted walls and hidden light, proof that austere modernism can be devotional.
projects.wikipedia: Church of Santa Maria (Marco de Canaveses)

projects.title: Faculty of Architecture, University of Porto
projects.blurb: The architecture school as a small acropolis of white pavilions above the Douro; a curriculum in built form.
projects.wikipedia: Faculty of Architecture of the University of Porto

projects.title: Galician Centre of Contemporary Art
projects.blurb: Granite-clad galleries negotiating a Baroque convent's garden wall in a UNESCO old town.

projects.title: Bouça Housing
projects.blurb: SAAL social housing rows begun with residents after the revolution, completed only in 2006.

projects.title: Bonjour Tristesse
projects.blurb: A curved gray IBA corner block in Kreuzberg, nicknamed by graffiti the architect chose to keep.

projects.title: Iberê Camargo Foundation
projects.blurb: A white museum with external ramps snaking over the facade, cantilevered toward the Guaíba; his first work in Brazil.

name: Michael Graves
bio: Graves began as the most painterly of the New York Five, then broke ranks with white abstraction for color, ornament and classical memory. The Portland Building (1982) — garlands, keystones, a copper Portlandia over the door — became America's first major postmodern public building, loved and loathed in roughly equal measure and repeatedly threatened with demolition. Humana in Louisville and the Swan and Dolphin hotels for Disney scaled the manner up; then came the teakettle, whose whistling bird for Alessi (1985) and some two thousand products for Target put his design in more American kitchens than any architect since. Paralyzed from the chest down by an infection in 2003, he spent his last decade designing hospitals, wheelchairs and accessible houses from a wheelchair, calling healthcare design his most important work. He taught at Princeton for almost four decades and died in 2015.

projects.title: Portland Building
projects.blurb: The first major postmodern public building in America — a decorated municipal box that launched a thousand arguments.

projects.title: Humana Building
projects.blurb: A pink granite corporate tower with a loggia and rooftop belvedere; postmodernism gone respectable.

projects.title: Denver Central Library
projects.blurb: A castle of colored volumes and a great derrick-topped rotunda anchoring the civic center.

projects.title: Walt Disney World Swan and Dolphin
projects.blurb: Turquoise waves, five-story swans and 17-meter dolphins; 'entertainment architecture' coined on the spot.
projects.wikipedia: Walt Disney World Swan and Dolphin

projects.title: Team Disney Burbank
projects.blurb: Disney's corporate headquarters with the Seven Dwarfs as caryatids holding up the pediment.

projects.title: San Juan Capistrano Library
projects.blurb: A small mission-inflected library of courtyards and light monitors; early proof the manner could be gentle.

projects.title: Snyderman House
projects.blurb: The most elaborate of his early layered-grid houses; lost to fire in 2002.

projects.title: Clos Pegase Winery
projects.blurb: A Napa winery as ocher temple complex, won in a museum-sponsored competition.

projects.title: Castalia, The Hague
projects.blurb: A ministry doubled into two steep-gabled towers — Dutch rooflines blown up to skyline scale.

projects.title: NCAA Headquarters and Hall of Champions
projects.blurb: A late civic commission in his hometown's White River State Park.

name: Richard Meier
bio: Meier took Le Corbusier's white villas of the 1920s and spent a career refining them — porcelain-enameled panels, layered grids, ramps, and light treated as the real building material. The Smith House of 1967 made his name; membership in the New York Five confirmed the allegiance to whiteness; the Pritzker arrived in 1984, when he was 49 and its youngest laureate. The Getty Center (1997), thirteen years and a billion dollars in the making, spread his manner across a Brentwood hilltop in travertine, while Frankfurt, Barcelona and Rome collected his museums. He was that rarity, a signature architect whose signature never wavered — critics called it repetition, clients called it reliability. In 2018 five women accused him of sexual harassment; he withdrew from practice, and the firm he founded in 1963 continues without his name at the door, as Meier Partners.

projects.title: Getty Center
projects.blurb: A billion-dollar acropolis of travertine and white metal above the 405; museum, institute and garden as one campus.

projects.title: High Museum of Art
projects.blurb: A white quadrant atrium ringed by ramps — the building that helped win his Pritzker the following year.

projects.title: Barcelona Museum of Contemporary Art
projects.blurb: A white light-box dropped into the medieval Raval, its plaza now as famous for skateboarding as for art.

projects.title: Smith House
projects.blurb: A white wood-framed house on the Long Island Sound rocks; the career's founding document.

projects.title: Douglas House
projects.blurb: A white machine moored to a steep Lake Michigan bluff, entered across a bridge to the roof.

projects.title: The Atheneum
projects.blurb: A visitors' center for a utopian settlement — ramps and skewed grids as a promenade above the Wabash.

projects.title: Jubilee Church
projects.blurb: Three concrete sails of self-cleaning white cement in a Roman suburb, built for the millennium.

projects.title: Museum Angewandte Kunst
projects.blurb: A decorative-arts museum gridded off a 19th-century villa on Frankfurt's museum embankment.

projects.title: 173 and 176 Perry Street
projects.blurb: Glass apartment towers on the West Village waterfront that made the celebrity condominium a genre.

projects.title: Ara Pacis Museum
projects.blurb: A glass and travertine pavilion for Augustus's altar of peace — the first modern building in Rome's center since the war, furiously contested.

name: Hans Hollein
bio: Hollein built almost nothing for a decade and it hardly mattered: his montages of aircraft carriers beached in wheat fields and his 1968 manifesto 'Alles ist Architektur' — everything, media and lipstick included, is architecture — made him famous first as a provocateur. The nine-square-meter Retti candle shop of 1965, an aluminum jewel box on Vienna's Kohlmarkt, won an American prize whose purse exceeded the construction cost. When the big commissions came he delivered: the Abteiberg museum at Mönchengladbach (1982) buried galleries in a terraced hillside and helped invent the museum as landscape, and the Haas House opposite St. Stephen's Cathedral scandalized Vienna before Vienna adopted it. Trained in Vienna, at IIT and at Berkeley, he was equally a designer, artist and exhibition-maker, and in 1985 became the only Austrian Pritzker laureate to date. He died in 2014; his children Max and Lilli went on to run the Metropolitan Museum and the MAK.

projects.title: Abteiberg Museum
projects.blurb: Galleries terraced into a hillside beneath a sculpture garden; the postmodern museum's founding building.

projects.title: Haas House
projects.blurb: A curved mirror-glass store facing the Gothic cathedral across Stephansplatz; Vienna's loudest architecture fight of the decade.

projects.title: Retti Candle Shop
projects.blurb: Nine square meters behind a slotted aluminum facade; the tiny shop that launched the career.

projects.title: Museum für Moderne Kunst
projects.blurb: A triangular museum wedged into a city block, nicknamed the 'slice of cake'.

projects.title: Vulcania

projects.title: Schullin Jewelry Shop
projects.blurb: A granite facade split by a gilded fissure — geology as shopfront, on the Graben.

projects.title: Interbank Headquarters

name: Kisho Kurokawa
bio: Kurokawa was twenty-six when he co-founded Metabolism in 1960, the movement that imagined cities growing and shedding parts like organisms, and he stayed its most visible evangelist for life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) — 140 prefabricated pods bolted to twin cores, designed to be swapped out every 25 years and never once replaced — became the movement's built manifesto and, after its 2022 demolition, its relic. A student of Kenzō Tange with a taste for philosophy, he repackaged Metabolism as 'symbiosis', wrote dozens of books, and appeared on television often enough to be a genuine celebrity. His late career went big: an airport in the Malaysian rainforest, stadiums, and the National Art Center in Tokyo, which opened months before his death. In 2007 he ran quixotically for governor of Tokyo, lost badly, and died that October at 73.

projects.title: Nakagin Capsule Tower
projects.blurb: 140 replaceable living capsules on two concrete cores; Metabolism's built manifesto, demolished in 2022.

projects.title: National Art Center, Tokyo
projects.blurb: Japan's largest exhibition space behind a billowing glass facade; opened months before his death.

projects.title: Kuala Lumpur International Airport
